reasoning: Both outputs are strong and both satisfy all four expectations — neither treats retry/skip/loosen as the fix, both frame the flake as an undeclared dependency in the system, both build a measurement harness before touching code, and both argue the shortcut down explicitly. B wins narrowly on three grounds. (1) It answers this specific prompt more squarely: its first substantive move is a flat refusal plus the three shortcuts and what each actually costs ('converts a 20% signal into a 0% signal'), whereas A's opening table lists quarantine-with-skip as 'Yes, if you need green today', which softens exactly the line the prompt is testing. (2) B carries better fix-stage machinery, the part A leaves abstract: the 4b gate ('write down what production change should make this test fail; would the edited test still fail for it? NO -> you loosened the assertion, revert') is the sharpest anti-shortcut device in either document; the mutation check (git stash the fix, confirm it goes red again) catches the false fix that a rate comparison alone can miss; the production-vs-test fork keyed on 'does the contract actually promise what the test asserts' is a discriminator A never draws; and it ships working waitFor implementations in TS and Python where A only names the principle. (3) B sets a stricter reproduction bar — one command at >=95% failure, written at the top of the ticket, versus A's >=50% — and reasons from the evidence's shape rather than a generic prior (a steady 20% implies something sampled per run, so clock/TZ knobs go last, not first). It does this in ~5,000 words against A's ~6,450, with almost no redundancy, while A restates its confidence math in section 2, section 10 and again in the Stress Test. A's real advantages are on the diagnosis-instrumentation side and they are genuine: it actually ran its own tooling against synthetic fixtures, found and fixed a broken YAML block, and said so; its CI-history forensics spots SHAs that went both red and green as free replay anchors; its Wilson intervals and greens-needed table ('at 20%, 14 consecutive greens for 95% confidence') directly defuse the 'I ran it ten times' fallacy that B only implicitly guards against; and it is admirably explicit that its Phase 1 gate is unmet so the hypotheses are priors, not findings. But A's order-bisect fallback advantage is offset by weaker fix guidance, and its extra length buys reference breadth (the six-runtime knob table) rather than a better path to a fixed test. An engineer handed both would reach a verified, non-coincidental fix faster with B.

CI-history forensics as a zero-new-runs first move; detecting a SHA that went both red and green gives a free, confirmed replay anchor

Wilson confidence interval plus a greens-needed table (20% rate -> 14 consecutive greens for 95% confidence) directly attacks the central trap of flake work: treating green-run count as a proxy for 'fixed'
Five hypotheses each stated with an explicit falsification clause, plus a re-rank table keyed to the literal CI error text
Explicitly declares its own Phase 1 gate unmet ('I am handing you the loop, not a verdict'), so priors are not mistaken for findings
order-bisect.sh includes a linear-shrink fallback for polluters that span both halves, and that path was tested
Six-runtime knob table with the honest note that rspec --bisect and go test -race make its own script unnecessary in those ecosystems
weaknesses: Opens by listing quarantine-with-skip as 'Yes, if you need green today', giving the escape hatch top billing on a prompt specifically testing whether the line holds
Reproduction gate of >=50% is materially weaker than a 95% bar for calling a flake deterministic
Fix guidance is a hierarchy of principles with no runnable code — waitFor, clock injection and seeding are named but not implemented
No equivalent of a mutation check: nothing verifies that reverting the fix brings the failure back
~28% longer, with real redundancy — the confidence math appears in section 2, is restated in section 10, and again in the Stress Test
Section 7's self-verification, while trust-building, is space spent on its own artifacts rather than the user's bug, and A concedes it proves nothing about the flake

strengths: Leads with an unambiguous refusal and a three-row table of what each shortcut actually costs, including the sharp framing that the measured 20% rate is the most valuable artifact in the bug and the shortcut throws it away
The 4b gate — name the production change this test should catch, make the edit, ask whether it would still catch it — is the single best defence against assertion-loosening disguised as a fix
Mutation check (stash the fix, confirm red returns) catches the 'fixed' test that was only perturbed, the failure mode that produces re-flaking three weeks later
Production-vs-test fork keyed on whether the contract actually promises what the test asserts, with 'the test was wrong' allowed exactly once and only with the contract written down
Distinguishes probe from fix throughout — cache.clear() and a 2s sleep are confirmations, explicitly not the remedy
Reasons from the evidence's shape: a steady 20% implies a per-run sampled cause, so clock/TZ knobs are ordered last rather than by generic prior
Ships working waitFor implementations in TypeScript and Python, plus the one narrow case where a fixed delay is legitimate
Stricter exit criterion (one command, >=95% failure, written at the top of the ticket) and a clean Definition of Done checklist
Plain-English glosses interleaved after each technical block rather than lumped into a trailing section
Stress Test names the real tension head-on — that refusing a direct instruction is itself a risk, and the pushback should arrive with the reproduction command in hand
weaknesses: order-bisect.sh is the weaker script: it gives up with 'polluter spans both halves' instead of a linear shrink, leaves $RUNNER unquoted, and fails_with treating any of REPEAT runs as red can mislead the search while the ordering is still partly flaky
Asserts the 95% and 200/200 thresholds without the sample-size arithmetic that justifies them; no confidence-interval reasoning
Does not claim to have run any of its own scripts, so the bisector's rough edges went uncaught
CI mining lacks A's both-red-and-green SHA trick, which can confirm the flake and hand over a replay anchor in one step
The 'no root cause' exit clause, though well-guarded, sits at the end where a fatigued reader reaches for it first
